file_name: Hall et al. - 2023 - Co designing an Integrated Health and Social Care Hub With and for Families Experiencing Adversity.txt

barriers.description: COVID-19 restrictions forced exclusive online engagement, limiting warm face-to-face contact and informal community interactions that the team relied on to build rapport and recruit participants.
barriers.justification: This constrained facilitation of user involvement and understanding of context of use by reducing opportunities for informal engagement and early relationship-building essential to formative research and user testing.
barriers.reference_excerpt: Stakeholder engagement was negatively impacted by the COVID-19 pandemic because Wyndham was a ‘hot spot’ for COVID-19 transmission ... This meant that families and practitioners were stretched, fatigued and had other priorities. We also had to exclusively engage stakeholders online which limited our engagement with community members in the early part of the project because we could not rely on ‘hanging out’ at community services or warm face-to-face connections with clients through Hub practitioners.

barriers.description: The co-design process required substantial facilitator and participant time, with facilitators meeting half a day before and after workshops and team members reporting difficulty juggling project commitments with work and caregiving.
barriers.justification: High time demands limited designers' capacity to plan, iterate and support rapid prototyping and testing, hindering integration of feedback, producing design solutions, and conducting iterative evaluation.
barriers.reference_excerpt: A substantial time investment was required to plan and execute the workshops and consultations. The facilitators met for half a day before and after each workshop for the 10-week period to plan and iterate the co-design workshop materials and process. All co-design team members said it was difficult to juggle their commitment to the project with other priorities (i.e., work and caregiving).

barriers.description: Practitioners on the design team still needed to complete routine workloads despite managerial support, reducing their available capacity to contribute to co-design activities.
barriers.justification: External organisational and workload constraints on practitioner stakeholders limited the team's ability to sustain multidisciplinary participation and undertake additional user testing, impeding coordination of the co-design team and evaluation efforts.
barriers.reference_excerpt: Even with supportive managers, however, practitioners on the design team still felt they needed to complete their routine workload, which is a barrier reported across studies [11, 45]. Balancing the time commitment of co-design team members with the need to undertake additional user testing is a challenge in co-design projects [43].

barriers.description: Mixed stakeholder dynamics created emotional and power-related tensions: community members found it hard to voice critical views and some practitioners felt threatened by participant critique.
barriers.justification: These emotional and power-differential issues hindered facilitation of user involvement and coordination within the multidisciplinary team by reducing psychological safety and open contribution, limiting authentic input and iterative critique.
barriers.reference_excerpt: Working in a mixed stakeholder team added complexity. One community representative said it was difficult to express critical views of services despite facilitation encouraging this. Likewise, despite the improvement focus of the design process, some practitioners were threatened by the critique brought about through the ‘emphasise’ phase.

barriers.description: Participant recruitment produced a sample disproportionately female and English-speaking, raising concerns the co-design outputs may not meet the needs of male caregivers and diverse communities.
barriers.justification: Limited participant diversity constrained the team's ability to manage user understanding and specify inclusive user requirements, reducing confidence that design solutions reflect the full range of local user needs.
barriers.reference_excerpt: Our sample was disproportionately female, spoke English as a main language and were aged 25 to 44 years old. ... The co-designed Hub may not adequately meet the needs of male caregivers and diverse communities because we primarily engaged with females who spoke English.

barriers.description: The team did not record detailed demographics of user testing, an oversight that limited the data available about who provided feedback during prototype testing.
barriers.justification: This data-collection oversight impeded the designers' ability to assess representativeness of testing, undermining efforts to manage evolving user understanding, evaluate designs across groups, and specify requirements for under-represented populations.
barriers.reference_excerpt: A second limitation is that we did not record detailed demographics of user testing; an oversight partly because we did not expect this tool to be so effective.
